claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing was performed on murine pancreatic duct cells, pancreatobiliary cells, and intrapancreatic bile duct cells using DBA+ lectin sorting.
source: Here, we performed single-cell RNA-sequencing to examine heterogeneity of murine pancreatic duct cells, pancreatobiliary cells, and intrapancreatic bile duct cells.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the methodology used in the study.

claim: An epithelial-mesenchymal transitory axis exists in three pancreatic duct subpopulations.
source: We describe an epithelial-mesenchymal transitory axis in our three pancreatic duct subpopulations and identify osteopontin as a regulator of this fate decision as well as human duct cell dedifferentiation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this finding from the study.

claim: Osteopontin regulates the epithelial-mesenchymal fate decision in pancreatic duct cells.
source: We describe an epithelial-mesenchymal transitory axis in our three pancreatic duct subpopulations and identify osteopontin as a regulator of this fate decision as well as human duct cell dedifferentiation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly identifies osteopontin's regulatory role.

claim: Osteopontin regulates human duct cell dedifferentiation.
source: We describe an epithelial-mesenchymal transitory axis in our three pancreatic duct subpopulations and identify osteopontin as a regulator of this fate decision as well as human duct cell dedifferentiation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding.

claim: Geminin plays a role in accumulation of DNA damage in the setting of chronic pancreatitis.
source: Our results further identify functional heterogeneity within pancreatic duct subpopulations by elucidating a role for geminin in accumulation of DNA damage in the setting of chronic pancreatitis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this finding.

claim: Pancreatic duct cells can serve as a cell of origin for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA).
source: They can serve as a cell of origin for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) (Bailey et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019) and have been implicated in the pathophysiology of multiple other diseases including cystic fibrosis (Wilschanski and Novak, 2013) and pancreatitis (Apte et al., 1997).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pancreatic duct cells have been implicated in the pathophysiology of cystic fibrosis.
source: They can serve as a cell of origin for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) (Bailey et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019) and have been implicated in the pathophysiology of multiple other diseases including cystic fibrosis (Wilschanski and Novak, 2013) and pancreatitis (Apte et al., 1997).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Pancreatic duct cells have been implicated in the pathophysiology of pancreatitis.
source: They can serve as a cell of origin for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) (Bailey et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019) and have been implicated in the pathophysiology of multiple other diseases including cystic fibrosis (Wilschanski and Novak, 2013) and pancreatitis (Apte et al., 1997).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is a risk factor for pancreatic cancer.
source: Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is a risk factor for pancreatic cancer.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cytokines and reactive oxygen species generated during chronic inflammation can cause DNA damage.
source: Studies have shown that cytokines and reactive oxygen species generated during chronic inflammation can cause DNA damage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The dataset contained 6813 cells after filtering out doublets and low-quality cells.
source: After filtering out doublets and low-quality cells (defined by low transcript counts), our dataset contained 6813 cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data processing results.

claim: Clustering analysis identified 16 distinct cell populations.
source: Clustering analysis identified 16 distinct cell populations with an average of 5345 transcripts per cell and 1908 genes per cell (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The average number of transcripts per cell was 5345.
source: Clustering analysis identified 16 distinct cell populations with an average of 5345 transcripts per cell and 1908 genes per cell (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis results.

claim: The average number of genes per cell was 1908.
source: Clustering analysis identified 16 distinct cell populations with an average of 5345 transcripts per cell and 1908 genes per cell (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis results.

claim: The dataset comprises 2 populations of ductal cells, a cluster of endothelial cells, 1 cluster of fibroblasts, and 12 immune cell clusters.
source: Our dataset comprises 2 populations of ductal cells, a cluster of endothelial cells, 1 cluster of fibroblasts, and 12 immune cell clusters.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the clustering results.

claim: Murine endocrine and acinar cells are not present in the dataset because they are not DBA+ cells.
source: As expected, murine endocrine and acinar cells are not present in our dataset because they are not DBA+ cells.
evidence: This is stated as an expected result based on the sorting strategy.

claim: DBA+Collagen I+ fibroblasts were identified by immunofluorescence.
source: We identified DBA+Collagen I+ fibroblasts and DBA+CD45+ immune cells by immunofluorescence (IF).
evidence: This is stated as a validation result using immunofluorescence.

claim: DBA+CD45+ immune cells were identified by immunofluorescence.
source: We identified DBA+Collagen I+ fibroblasts and DBA+CD45+ immune cells by immunofluorescence (IF).
evidence: This is stated as a validation result using immunofluorescence.

claim: CD31+ endothelial cells are not DBA+.
source: CD31+ endothelial cells are not DBA+.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunofluorescence.

claim: The presence of CD31+ endothelial cells in the dataset might be explained by the close juxtaposition of pancreatic duct cells with endothelial cells throughout the murine pancreas.
source: Their presence in our dataset might be explained by the close juxtaposition of pancreatic duct cells with endothelial cells throughout the murine pancreas (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for an unexpected finding.

claim: Six distinct ductal clusters were revealed when analyzing all duct cells (clusters 0 and 8).
source: To get a better understanding of duct cell heterogeneity, we generated an Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plot using all duct cells (clusters 0 and 8), which revealed six distinct ductal clusters.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claim: Fewer murine duct cells express the transcription factor Hnf1b when compared to Sox9.
source: Notably, fewer murine duct cells express the transcription factor Hnf1b when compared to Sox9.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Cluster 0 contains the most cells of all duct clusters in the dataset.
source: Cluster 0 contains the most cells of all duct clusters in the dataset (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by source data.

claim: Mmd2, Kcne3, and Cftr were significantly upregulated in cluster 0 when compared to all other ductal clusters.
source: A gene that positively regulates Ras signaling Mmd2, the voltage-gated potassium channel protein encoded by Kcne3, as well as the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter chloride channel protein encoded by Cftr, were significantly upregulated in cluster 0 when compared to all other ductal clusters (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and source data.

claim: Cluster 0 shows upregulation or activation of multiple genes whose alteration play important roles in the pathophysiology of human pancreatic diseases.
source: Notably, cluster 0 shows upregulation or activation of multiple genes whose alteration play important roles in the pathophysiology of human pancreatic diseases such as CFTR for hereditary CP (Raphael and Willingham, 2016) and TGFB2 and CTNNB1 for pancreatic cancer (Shen et al., 2017; Gordon et al., 2008; Heiser et al., 2008; Figure 2—source data 1 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations and source data.

claim: CFTR alterations play an important role in hereditary chronic pancreatitis.
source: Notably, cluster 0 shows upregulation or activation of multiple genes whose alteration play important roles in the pathophysiology of human pancreatic diseases such as CFTR for hereditary CP (Raphael and Willingham, 2016) and TGFB2 and CTNNB1 for pancreatic cancer (Shen et al., 2017; Gordon et al., 2008; Heiser et al., 2008; Figure 2—source data 1 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TGFB2 and CTNNB1 alterations play important roles in pancreatic cancer.
source: Notably, cluster 0 shows upregulation or activation of multiple genes whose alteration play important roles in the pathophysiology of human pancreatic diseases such as CFTR for hereditary CP (Raphael and Willingham, 2016) and TGFB2 and CTNNB1 for pancreatic cancer (Shen et al., 2017; Gordon et al., 2008; Heiser et al., 2008; Figure 2—source data 1 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GMNN protein expression is rare in pancreatic duct cells despite widespread RNA expression.
source: Gmnn, an inhibitor of DNA replication, was expressed in both clusters 0 and 2, so we decided to examine histologically and were surprised to find rare GMNN protein expression, which was in contrast to the widespread RNA expression depicted by the feature plot (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from histological examination compared to RNA-seq data.

claim: GMNN expression is very low or absent in human main pancreatic ducts.
source: After examining more than 1500 main pancreatic duct cells from five donors, we were unable to find a GMNN-positive cell, indicating very low or absent expression of GMNN in human main pancreatic ducts.
evidence: This is stated as a result from examining human tissue samples.

claim: Spp1 and Wfdc3 show cytoplasmic protein expression in all mouse and human pancreatic duct types.
source: Spp1, which encodes osteopontin, and Wfdc3, which are significantly DEGs in both clusters 0 and 2, show cytoplasmic protein expression in all mouse and human pancreatic duct types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result from immunohistochemistry validation.

claim: Cells in cluster 1 have significantly upregulated expression of Rab27b and Ppp1r1b.
source: Cells in cluster 1 have significantly upregulated expression of the exosome biogenesis gene Rab27b as well as Ppp1r1b that encodes for a molecule with kinase and phosphatase inhibition activity (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and source data.

claim: IPA results suggested an enrichment in molecules regulating Calcium Transport I in cluster 1.
source: IPA results suggested an enrichment in molecules regulating Calcium Transport I (Figure 2D and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result from pathway analysis.

claim: Intracellular calcium signaling in pancreatic duct cells is an important regulator of homeostatic bicarbonate secretion.
source: Intracellular calcium signaling in pancreatic duct cells is an important regulator of homeostatic bicarbonate secretion (Maléth and Hegyi, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PPP1R1B, SMARCA4, and TGFB1 have well-described roles in the pathogenesis of pancreatic cancer.
source: PPP1R1B, SMARCA4, and TGFB1 have well-described roles in the pathogenesis of pancreatic cancer (Roy et al., 2015; David et al., 2016; Tiwari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Anxa3 and Pah show cytoplasmic protein expression in all mouse and human pancreatic duct types.
source: We observed expression of markers of cluster 1, Anxa3 and Pah, which are also DEGs in cluster 4, to have cytoplasmic protein expression in all mouse and human pancreatic duct types (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result from immunohistochemistry validation.

claim: Co-staining of CFTR and ANXA3 shows both overlapping and non-overlapping patterns of expression in human intercalated ducts.
source: Co-staining of CFTR, a marker of cluster 0, and ANXA3 shows both overlapping and non-overlapping patterns of expression in human intercalated ducts, validating the heterogeneity observed in our murine pancreatic duct dataset in human pancreatic duct cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated as a validation result from immunofluorescence.

claim: Cluster 2 is characterized by low level or lack of expression of multiple ductal cell markers found in other clusters.
source: Cluster 2 is characterized by low level or lack of expression of multiple ductal cell markers (Cftr, Kcne3, Sparc, Mmd2, Krt7) found in other clusters (Figure 2B, C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Cluster 2 has the lowest average expression of total genes and transcripts.
source: Cluster 2 has the lowest average expression of total genes and transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and source data.

claim: Cluster 2 represents a stable, fairly transcriptionally and metabolically inactive duct cell subpopulation when compared to other duct clusters.
source: We therefore posit that cluster 2 represents a stable, fairly transcriptionally and metabolically inactive duct cell subpopulation when compared to other duct clusters.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Cluster 3 cells are located almost entirely within cluster 8 of the UMAP containing 16 DBA+ clusters.
source: Cluster 3 cells are located almost entirely within cluster 8 of the UMAP containing 16 DBA+ clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure.

claim: Cluster 3 was identified as intrapancreatic bile duct cells based on high expression of genes regulating cilia biogenesis.
source: This, along with high expression of genes regulating cilia biogenesis (Foxj1, Cfap44, Tuba1a), led to the identification of cluster 3 as intrapancreatic bile duct cells (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result from gene expression analysis.

claim: Expression of cilia biogenesis genes is more prominent in intrapancreatic bile duct cells when compared to pancreatic duct cells.
source: Expression of cilia biogenesis genes is more prominent in intrapancreatic bile duct cells when compared to pancreatic duct cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, Figure 2—source data 1, and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Cells in cluster 4 have significantly higher expression of Tgfb3 and Dclk1 when compared to all other ductal clusters.
source: Cells in cluster 4 have significantly higher expression of Tgfb3 and Dclk1 when compared to all other ductal clusters (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and source data.

claim: DCLK1 labels tuft cells that are present in normal murine intrapancreatic bile ducts and pancreatobiliary ductal epithelium.
source: DCLK1 labels tuft cells that are present in normal murine intrapancreatic bile ducts, pancreatobiliary ductal epithelium (DelGiorno et al., 2014), and rare normal murine pancreatic duct cells (Westphalen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: YAP1 is essential for homeostasis of biliary duct cells.
source: YAP1, a transcriptional regulator essential for homeostasis of biliary duct cells (Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019), was predicted to be in an activated state by IPA upstream regulator analysis (Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cluster 4 contained a small population (13 cells) of Dmbt1 and Ly6d-expressing cells previously identified in extrahepatic biliary epithelium.
source: Cluster 4 also contained a small population (13 cells) of Dmbt1 and Ly6d-expressing cells previously identified in extrahepatic biliary epithelium (Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation and figure.

claim: Cluster 4 contains pancreatobiliary duct cells based on shared features with both bile and pancreas ducts.
source: Based on these shared features of bile and pancreas ducts, we postulate that cluster 4 contains pancreatobiliary duct cells.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Replicating duct cells comprise 1.65% of all duct cells in the dataset.
source: Replicating duct cells are characterized by high expression of Mki67, Cenpf, and Cenpe and comprise 1.65% of all duct cells in our dataset (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and source data.

claim: Pancreatic duct cells are fairly mitotically inactive.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Moin et al., 2017; Butler et al., 2010), pancreatic duct cells are fairly mitotically inactive.
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with previous literature.

claim: Dendrogram analysis, Pearson's correlation, and DEGs revealed close relationships between clusters 0 and 2 as well as clusters 1 and 4.
source: Dendrogram analysis, Pearson's correlation, and DEGs revealed close relationships between clusters 0 and 2 as well as clusters 1 and 4 (Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and source data.

claim: Comparison of clusters 0 and 2 showed only nine significant DEGs, suggesting a shared core gene expression program.
source: Comparison of clusters 0 and 2 showed only nine significant DEGs, suggesting a shared core gene expression program (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Overrepresentation of molecules regulating the cell cycle was observed in cluster 0 when compared to cluster 2.
source: Overrepresentation of molecules regulating the cell cycle was observed in cluster 0 when compared to cluster 2 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure.

claim: Cluster 0 comprises workhorse pancreatic duct cells based on upregulation of genes that promote duct cell function.
source: The DEGs upregulated in cluster 0 promote duct cell function (Cftr, Tuba1a, Kcne3), suggesting that cluster 0 comprises workhorse pancreatic duct cells (Hayashi and Novak, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data supported by a citation.

claim: Pancreatobiliary cells show enrichment in expression of genes regulating assembly of cell junctions when compared to pancreatic duct cells in cluster 1.
source: When comparing pancreatobiliary cells of cluster 4 to pancreatic duct cells in cluster 1, one of the most striking differences is the enrichment in expression of genes regulating assembly of cell junctions including tight junctions, epithelial adherens junction signaling, regulation of actin-based motility by Rho, and actin cytoskeleton signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a result from pathway analysis.

claim: Cluster 4: Dmbt1+Ly6d+ cells are characterized by strong upregulation of pathways regulating xenobiotic metabolism when compared to all other cluster 4 cells.
source: Cluster 4: Dmbt1+Ly6d+ cells are characterized by strong upregulation of pathways regulating xenobiotic metabolism when compared to all other cluster 4 cells, suggesting a prominent role for these cells in the bile acid and xenobiotic system (BAXS) (Figure 3I–K and Figure 3—source data 2 and 3; Dubitzky et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures, source data, and a citation.

claim: Intrapancreatic bile duct cells primarily cluster together with hepatic BECs expressing subpopulation B genes.
source: Intrapancreatic bile duct cells primarily cluster together with hepatic BECs expressing subpopulation B genes, and pancreatobiliary cells primarily cluster together with hepatic BECs expressing subpopulation A genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result from alignment analysis with hepatic BEC data.

claim: Pancreatobiliary cells primarily cluster together with hepatic BECs expressing subpopulation A genes.
source: Intrapancreatic bile duct cells primarily cluster together with hepatic BECs expressing subpopulation B genes, and pancreatobiliary cells primarily cluster together with hepatic BECs expressing subpopulation A genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result from alignment analysis with hepatic BEC data.

claim: Distinct subpopulations of ductal cells that overlap in expression of key marker genes associated with adult pancreas ductal subpopulations are evident during pancreas development at E12.5, E14.5, and E17.5.
source: We found distinct subpopulations of ductal cells that notably overlap in expression of key marker genes associated with adult pancreas ductal subpopulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–L).
evidence: This is stated as a result from analysis of developmental datasets.

claim: Clear patterns of marker gene expression associated with adult clusters manifest at later stages of development.
source: As we expected, clear patterns of marker gene expression associated with adult clusters manifest at later stages of development (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, H, L).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from developmental data analysis.

claim: The subpopulations of adult pancreas duct cells described in C57BL/6J mice are conserved in Swiss Webster mice.
source: Since the developmental biology samples were obtained from Swiss Webster mice, our results suggest the subpopulations of adult pancreas duct cells we describe in C57BL/6J mice are conserved.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the developmental data analysis.

claim: Murine pancreatic duct clusters 0–2 had the highest scores when compared to human ALK3+ clusters 1 and 2.
source: Murine pancreatic duct clusters 0–2 had the highest scores when compared to human ALK3+ clusters 1 (OPN+stress/harboring progenitor-like cells) and 2 (TFF1+ activated/migrating progenitor cells).
evidence: This is stated as a result from AddModuleScore analysis.

claim: Murine pancreatobiliary cells (cluster 4) scored the highest when compared to the human ALK3+ cluster 3.
source: Murine pancreatobiliary cells (cluster 4) scored the highest when compared to the human ALK3+ cluster 3 (AKAP12+ small ducts).
evidence: This is stated as a result from AddModuleScore analysis.

claim: DBA is expressed in murine centroacinar/terminal ducts as early as 3 weeks of age.
source: DBA is expressed in murine centroacinar/terminal ducts as early as 3 weeks of age (Stanger et al., 2005), thus these cells would be expected to be present in our dataset (Beer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DBA+CPA1+ and DBA+α-amylase+ ducto-acinar cells were identified in adult murine pancreas.
source: Although ducto-acinar cells, like centroacinar/terminal ductal cells, do not define a unique cluster in our DBA+ murine duct subpopulations, we identified DBA+CPA1+ and DBA+α-amylase+ ducto-acinar cells in adult murine pancreas (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is stated as a result from immunolabeling.

claim: Murine centroacinar/terminal ductal and ducto-acinar cells are largely transcriptionally homogenous with other murine duct cell types.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that murine centroacinar/terminal ductal and ducto-acinar cells are largely transcriptionally homogenous with other murine duct cell types.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: RaceID3 clusters with the highest StemID2 score correlate to cells present in Seurat duct clusters 0 and 2.
source: RaceID3 clusters with the highest StemID2 score correlate to cells present in Seurat duct clusters 0 and 2 (Figure 4C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from RaceID3/StemID2 analysis.

claim: The variable StemID2 scores observed for cells within Seurat duct clusters 0, 1, 2, and 4 suggest distinct stages of differentiation or maturation.
source: The variable StemID2 scores observed for cells within Seurat duct clusters 0, 1, 2, and 4 suggest distinct stages of differentiation or maturation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the StemID2 analysis.

claim: The pancreatic ductal cell progenitor niche is not restricted to a single cluster.
source: Consistent with previous literature, the pancreatic ductal cell progenitor niche is not restricted to a single cluster (Qadir et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with previous literature.

claim: Monocle 3 analysis suggested DBA+ duct clusters 3 and 5 were disconnected from the main pseudotime trajectory.
source: Monocle 3 analysis suggested DBA+ duct clusters 3 and 5 were disconnected from the main pseudotime trajectory, so we focused our analysis on DBA+ duct clusters 0, 1, 2, and 4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from Monocle 3 analysis.

claim: A shift in the molecules driving the xenobiotic metabolism CAR signaling pathway was observed between modules 4 and 14.
source: Examination of pathways deregulated in modules 4 and 14 showed a shift in the molecules driving the xenobiotic metabolism CAR signaling pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a result from pathway analysis of Monocle 3 modules.

claim: The xenobiotic nuclear receptor CAR is an important sensor of physiologic toxins and plays a role in their removal.
source: The xenobiotic nuclear receptor CAR is an important sensor of physiologic toxins and plays a role in their removal (Timsit and Negishi, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Regulation of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition by growth factors pathway was upregulated in cluster 1 when compared to cluster 0 in module 34.
source: Regulation of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition by growth factors pathway was upregulated in cluster 1 when compared to cluster 0 in module 34.
evidence: This is stated as a result from pathway analysis.

claim: Vimentin+, SNAI1+, and fibronectin+ ductal cells were detected in both mouse and human pancreas.
source: Using IF, we detected vimentin+, SNAI1+, and fibronectin+ ductal cells in both mouse and human pancreas, providing evidence for this EMT axis (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a validation result from immunofluorescence.

claim: Spp1 has been shown to mark a pancreas duct cell type enriched in progenitor capacity.
source: Spp1, a marker of clusters 0 and 2, has been shown by us and others to mark a pancreas duct cell type enriched in progenitor capacity (Qadir et al., 2020; Kilic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Anxa3 inhibits phospholipase A2 and cleaves inositol 1,2-cyclic phosphate-generating inositol 1-phosphate in a calcium-dependent manner.
source: Anxa3, a marker of clusters 1 and 4, inhibits phospholipase A2 and cleaves inositol 1,2-cyclic phosphate-generating inositol 1-phosphate in a calcium-dependent manner (Tait et al., 1993; Gerke and Moss, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gmnn acts to inhibit re-replication of DNA during DNA synthesis by inhibiting the prereplication complex.
source: Gmnn, a marker of cluster 0, acts to inhibit re-replication of DNA during DNA synthesis by inhibiting the prereplication complex (McGarry and Kirschner, 1998; Ballabeni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HPDE6c7 cells demonstrate several features of normal pancreatic duct epithelium including gene expression of MUC1, CA2, and KRT19.
source: HPDE6c7 cells demonstrate several features of normal pancreatic duct epithelium including gene expression of MUC1, CA2, and KRT19 and have been used in many investigations as an in vitro model of 'near normal' human pancreatic duct cells (Ouyang et al., 2000; Furukawa et al., 1996; Qian et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells displayed a dramatic change in cellular morphology with prominent filipodia.
source: HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells showed prominent filipodia and significantly increased proliferation when compared to the HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control, a phenotype suggestive of increased progenitor function (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from cell culture experiments.

claim: HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells showed significantly increased proliferation when compared to the HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control.
source: HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells showed prominent filipodia and significantly increased proliferation when compared to the HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control, a phenotype suggestive of increased progenitor function (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is stated as a result from cell counting experiments.

claim: The change in cellular morphology in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines is accompanied by decreased duct function as measured by carbonic anhydrase activity.
source: The change in cellular morphology in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines is accompanied by decreased duct function as measured by carbonic anhydrase activity (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated as a result from carbonic anhydrase activity assays.

claim: A significant increase in markers associated with EMT was observed in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines when compared to the control.
source: A significant increase in markers associated with EMT (VIM, ZEB1, TWIST1, MMP2) was observed in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines when compared to the control (Figure 6—source data 1–4, Figure 6G–H, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from bulk RNA-sequencing.

claim: Markers of mature duct cells (HNF1B, SOX9, KRT19) were significantly downregulated in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines when compared to the control.
source: Markers of mature duct cells (HNF1B, SOX9, KRT19) were significantly downregulated in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines when compared to the control (Figure 6G, I, J and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result from bulk RNA-sequencing and immunocytochemistry.

claim: GSEA suggested positive enrichment of pathways that regulate embryogenesis (Hox genes and Notch signaling) and cell cycle regulation in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines when compared to the HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) suggested positive enrichment of pathways that regulate embryogenesis (Hox genes and Notch signaling) and cell cycle regulation in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines when compared to the HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is stated as a result from GSEA analysis.

claim: A significant increase in pancreatic progenitor markers was observed in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines when compared to the HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control.
source: Additionally, qPCR analysis demonstrated a significant increase in pancreatic progenitor markers (Gu et al., 2004; Willmann et al., 2016) in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines when compared to the HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control, supporting the notion that loss of OPN leads to a more immature, progenitor-like state (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is stated as a result from qPCR analysis.

claim: Loss of OPN leads to a more immature, progenitor-like state in human pancreatic duct cells.
source: Additionally, qPCR analysis demonstrated a significant increase in pancreatic progenitor markers (Gu et al., 2004; Willmann et al., 2016) in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO lines when compared to the HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control, supporting the notion that loss of OPN leads to a more immature, progenitor-like state (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the qPCR results.

claim: Transdifferentiation of pancreatic duct cells to endocrine cells at early postnatal stages and in pancreatic injury models has been suggested by several studies.
source: Transdifferentiation of pancreatic duct cells to endocrine cells at early postnatal stages and in pancreatic injury models has been suggested by several studies (Bonner-Weir et al., 2008; Kim and Lee, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: α-amylase+ CK19+ double-positive cells were evident in HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control cells at 5 days post-injection, but not in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells.
source: After 5 days post-injection, α-amylase+ CK19+ double-positive cells were evident in HPDE6c7 scr gRNA control cells, but not in HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from in vivo experiments.

claim: Neurogenin-3+SOX9+ copositive HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells were observed, suggesting potential for differentiation towards the endocrine lineage.
source: We observed Neurogenin-3+SOX9+ copositive HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells, suggesting potential for differentiation towards the endocrine lineage (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from in vivo experiments with an interpretation.

claim: Synaptophysin+ Glucagon+ as well as Synaptophysin+ C-peptide+ double-positive HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells were detected.
source: We detected Synaptophysin+ Glucagon+ as well as Synaptophysin+ C-peptide+ double-positive HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: This is stated as a result from in vivo experiments.

claim: A small subset of C-peptide+ HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells express both PDX1 and NKX6.1.
source: A small subset of C-peptide+ HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells express both PDX1 and NKX6.1 (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: This is stated as a result from in vivo experiments.

claim: SPP1 plays previously unappreciated roles in maintaining duct cell properties and preventing changes in cell identity.
source: Together, these data point to previously unappreciated roles for SPP1 in maintaining duct cell properties and preventing changes in cell identity.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the in vivo experimental results.

claim: Geminin expression in human pancreas duct cells is significantly increased in CP patients when compared to normal human pancreatic duct cells.
source: We examined proliferation in human pancreas duct cells in CP patients (N = 5 patients) and found a significant increase in geminin expression when compared to normal human pancreatic duct cells (N = 10 donors) (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: Pancreatic duct ligation (PDL) results in an increase in proliferation of rat pancreatic duct cells.
source: Pancreatic duct ligation (PDL), an experimental technique that recapitulates features of human gallstone pancreatitis, results in an increase in proliferation of rat pancreatic duct cells (Githens, 1988; Walker and Pound, 1983).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Upregulation of Geminin in ductal epithelium was observed in the control PDL mouse group.
source: As in the human setting, we also observed upregulation of Geminin in ductal epithelium in the control PDL mouse group (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the PDL experiments.

claim: Significant attenuation of Geminin expression was observed in Sox9-CreERT2Tg/wt; Gemininf/f, Sox9-CreERT2Tg/wt; Gemininf/wt, and Hnf1bCreERT2 Tg/wt; Gemininf/f mouse pancreatic duct cells when compared to controls.
source: Significant attenuation of Geminin expression was observed in Sox9-CreERT2Tg/wt; Gemininf/f, Sox9-CreERT2Tg/wt; Gemininf/wt, and Hnf1bCreERT2 Tg/wt; Gemininf/f mouse pancreatic duct cells when compared to controls (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the PDL experiments.

claim: Homozygous Gmnn loss in SOX9+ pancreatic ductal cells promoted an acute increase in proliferation at day 7, which became insignificant at day 30.
source: Homozygous Gmnn loss in SOX9+ pancreatic ductal cells promoted an acute increase in proliferation, as assessed by BrdU incorporation, at day 7, which became insignificant at day 30 (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B-E).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the PDL experiments.

claim: Significantly increased γ-H2AX foci were observed in Sox9-CreERT2Tg/wt; Gemininf/f mice at day 7, an observation that was sustained at day 30.
source: Examination of duct cell DNA damage by γ-H2AX IF showed significantly increased γ-H2AX foci in Sox9-CreERT2Tg/wt; Gemininf/f mice at day 7, an observation that was sustained at day 30 (Figure 8E–H).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the PDL experiments.

claim: Geminin is an important regulator of genomic stability in pancreatic duct cells in the setting of CP.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Geminin is an important regulator of genomic stability in pancreatic ducta cells in the setting of CP.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the PDL experimental results.

claim: The single-cell analysis indicated that endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells are also obtained using the DBA+ lectin sorting strategy.
source: Notably, our single-cell analysis indicated that endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells are also obtained using the DBA+ lectin sorting strategy (Reichert et al., 2013) and suggests that a subsequent ductal purification step is required to obtain pure pancreatic duct cells using this protocol.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the single-cell analysis.

claim: A subsequent ductal purification step is required to obtain pure pancreatic duct cells using the DBA+ lectin sorting protocol.
source: Notably, our single-cell analysis indicated that endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells are also obtained using the DBA+ lectin sorting strategy (Reichert et al., 2013) and suggests that a subsequent ductal purification step is required to obtain pure pancreatic duct cells using this protocol.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation based on the findings.

claim: Cluster 0 workhorse pancreatic duct cells comprise the largest pancreatic duct subpopulation identified.
source: Cluster 0 workhorse pancreatic duct cells comprise the largest pancreatic duct subpopulation identified.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: IPA suggested that subpopulations of pancreatic duct cells may use different predominant mechanisms for bicarbonate secretion.
source: IPA suggested that subpopulations of pancreatic duct cells may use different predominant mechanisms for bicarbonate secretion such as CFTR (Ishiguro et al., 2009) for cluster 0 and calcium signaling for cluster 1 (Ishiguro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the IPA results supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that distinct ductal cell subpopulations that are actively expressing certain pathways may have different predispositions to PDA with mutations in these genes.
source: These genes play central roles in homeostasis of pancreatic duct cells, and it is possible that distinct ductal cell subpopulations that are actively expressing these pathways may have different predispositions to PDA with mutations in these genes, heterogeneity which may also contribute to the development of different subtypes of PDA.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Spp1 KO mice have no apparent pancreatic duct phenotypes.
source: The role of Spp1 in homeostatic pancreatic duct cells has been elusive since Spp1 KO mice have no apparent pancreatic duct phenotypes (Kilic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Clusters 0 and 2, characterized by strong expression of Spp1, show the highest StemID2 scores.
source: Clusters 0 and 2, characterized by strong expression of Spp1, show the highest StemID2 scores.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the StemID2 analysis.

claim: SPP1 loss promotes human duct cell dedifferentiation.
source: Taken together, these phenotypes, along with upregulation of pathways regulating mammalian development (Notch signaling and Hox genes) manifested by GSEA, suggest that SPP1 loss promotes human duct cell dedifferentiation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: OPN-deficient HPDE6c7 cells dedifferentiate into a trunk, and not tip, progenitor-like cell.
source: Our data suggest that OPN-deficient HPDE6c7 cells dedifferentiate into a trunk, and not tip, progenitor-like cell and that redifferentiation of HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells to a human pancreatic duct or acinar cell lineage is not favored in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the in vivo experimental results.

claim: Redifferentiation of HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells to a human pancreatic duct or acinar cell lineage is not favored in vivo.
source: Our data suggest that OPN-deficient HPDE6c7 cells dedifferentiate into a trunk, and not tip, progenitor-like cell and that redifferentiation of HPDE6c7 SPP1 KO cells to a human pancreatic duct or acinar cell lineage is not favored in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the in vivo experimental results.

claim: OPN expression is required for mature human pancreas duct cell identity.
source: These data underscore the requirement for OPN expression for mature human pancreas duct cell identity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Spp1 plays important roles in pancreatic pathologies including PDA.
source: Several groups have already nicely shown that Spp1 plays important roles in pancreatic pathologies including PDA (Adams et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: 13 out of 14 cancer-related pathways were in a direction suggestive that SPP1 loss protects against tumor progression in human pancreatic duct cells.
source: 13/14 of these cancer-related pathways, including pancreatic adenocarcinoma signaling, were in a direction suggestive that SPP1 loss protects against tumor progression in human pancreatic duct cells.
evidence: This is stated as a result from IPA pathway analysis.

claim: SPP1 loss ameliorates aggressiveness of pancreatic cancer cells.
source: These findings are in agreement with published studies suggesting that SPP1 loss ameliorates aggressiveness of pancreatic cancer cells (Kolb et al., 2005; Adams et al., 2019) and colon cancer cells (Zhao et al., 2018; Ishigamori et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The requirement for Geminin in the prevention of DNA re-replication initiation has been postulated to be when cells are stressed to divide quickly.
source: The requirement for Geminin in the prevention of DNA re-replication initiation has been postulated to be when cells are stressed to divide quickly (Barry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Compensatory mechanisms with redundant function, such as ubiquitin-dependent degradation of CDT1 at the time of replication licensing, may exist in homeostatic pancreatic duct cells.
source: We were unable to detect DNA damage with Geminin loss in homeostatic pancreatic duct cells, which may be due to the low proliferation rate of pancreatic duct cells and/or the presence of compensatory mechanisms with redundant function, such as ubiquitin-dependent degradation of CDT1 at the time of replication licensing (Arias and Walter, 2005; Kerns et al., 2007; Li and Blow, 2005; Maiorano et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation supported by citations.

claim: Compensatory mechanisms are not sufficient to rescue the effects of Geminin loss in pancreatic duct cells in the context of CP.
source: Compensatory mechanisms are not sufficient to rescue the effects of Geminin loss in pancreatic duct cells in the context of CP, the result of which is accumulation of sustained DNA damage evident by γ-H2AX, but not ATR labeling.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: ATR is activated in Geminin-depleted colon cancer cell lines.
source: It has been previously reported that ATR is activated in Geminin-depleted colon cancer cell lines (Lin and Dutta, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Activation of the ATR-CHK1 pathway is not a major player in pancreatic duct cells in the setting of CP.
source: Activation of the ATR-CHK1 pathway is not a major player in pancreatic duct cells in the setting of CP (Smith et al., 2010), suggesting that different mechanisms participate in sensing Geminin depletion-induced DNA damage in different experimental systems and tissues.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Different mechanisms participate in sensing Geminin depletion-induced DNA damage in different experimental systems and tissues.
source: Activation of the ATR-CHK1 pathway is not a major player in pancreatic duct cells in the setting of CP (Smith et al., 2010), suggesting that different mechanisms participate in sensing Geminin depletion-induced DNA damage in different experimental systems and tissues.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the comparison of findings.
